summary: SQLite WAL checkpointing copies committed page changes from the write-ahead log into the main database while preserving readers' snapshots. Copying pages, making the WAL reusable, and truncating its file are separate outcomes. SQLite normally runs passive automatic checkpoints; applications can select stronger modes for completion or reclamation. Long-lived readers and overlapping checkpoints can prevent progress, so operators must inspect checkpoint results rather than infer success from file size. Scheduling trades commit latency against WAL growth. A documented WAL-reset corruption race also makes the engine's patched version relevant to aggressive manual checkpointing.

claims.text: Checkpointing copies eligible committed page versions from the WAL into the main database; it is separate from committing a transaction and from truncating the WAL.
A reader's snapshot limits checkpoint progress. Long-running or continuously overlapping readers can prevent WAL recycling and permit unbounded growth; later checkpoints resume partial work.

Automatic checkpoints are PASSIVE and run after commits once the per-connection WAL threshold is reached; the default is 1000 frames, configurable through wal_autocheckpoint, with nonpositive values disabling it.
PASSIVE checkpoints do available work without waiting for readers or writers; they never invoke the busy handler and can finish with frames still uncheckpointed.
FULL waits for the writer to finish and readers to use the newest snapshot, then copies all frames and syncs the database; it blocks concurrent writers.
RESTART adds waiting for readers to stop using the WAL, ensuring the next writer can reuse it; TRUNCATE additionally reduces the WAL file to zero bytes on successful completion.

wal_checkpoint returns busy status, WAL-frame count, and checkpointed-frame count. For PASSIVE, comparing the counts reveals incomplete work even when status is zero. An absent WAL yields -1 counts; NOOP reads counts without checkpointing.

Concurrent checkpoints compete for an exclusive checkpoint lock; contention returns SQLITE_BUSY without calling the busy handler. If FULL/RESTART/TRUNCATE exhaust their busy handler while waiting for writers or readers, they perform available passive work and return SQLITE_BUSY.

The commit that crosses the automatic-checkpoint threshold normally runs the checkpoint in its own thread, so some commits take longer; applications can disable autocheckpointing and schedule checkpoints separately.

SQLite documents a rare WAL-reset race between checkpointing and concurrent writes that can lose committed pages and corrupt the database. The fix is in 3.51.3 and selected backports; Tailscale encountered it with aggressive manual checkpoints.

sources.title: How we tracked down a 16-year-old SQLite bug

disagreements.text: Fly describes RESTART/TRUNCATE as blocking new reads and writes. SQLite's PRAGMA documentation allows readers to proceed, while its WAL guide warns of possible reader blocking; neither description establishes a universal reader-latency guarantee.

open_questions: Which checkpoint interval, reader-transaction bound, and busy-handler policy meet a particular workload's latency and WAL-size limits?
Which VFS and locking configurations explain the differences in the sources' statements about reader blocking during RESTART/TRUNCATE checkpoints?
